references.title: Deviations from preregistration Deviations are classified following Lakens

We hypothesised that craving would increase during the detox (H3), but the analysis plan specified only a pre/post-detox mixed ANOVA, which tests change after the detox. No analysis was specified for change during the detox

We had envisioned to also run a between-group version of this test, but this was not possible because the craving questionnaire was left out of the waitlist group's BL1 survey through an administrative error. Without a concurrent control group, the within-subject test cannot separate an effect of the detox from changes over time

> Participants were recruited through the university network and paid advertisements on Facebook and Instagram.

> This amended stopping rule described that enrolment would cease after 120 participants had completed the first three weekly questionnaires, based on an expected 15% attrition rate thereafter.

> This number is slightly higher than the target of 120 because some participants were already partway through the study when the enrolment threshold was reached, consistent with the anticipated attrition buffer.

> Participants were randomly assigned to either an immediate detox group or a waitlist group.

> During baseline week(s), participants were instructed to use social media as usual.

> Participants were free to remove additional apps if they wished.

> Participants completed the SRBAI only if they reported using social media in the past week.

> Participants completed three self-report measures related to their psychological functioning at each survey timepoint.

> As preregistered, participants were invited to complete follow-up surveys post-detox, including the same questionnaires as the weekly surveys (with weekly rather than daily screentime metrics).

> At baseline (T0), participants completed a survey that included questions on demographics (gender, age, education, employment), and open-ended questions about how they used social media.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: The effect of a Digital Detox on social media use, craving and automaticity
table.data_collection_started: It's complicated. We have already collected some data but explain in Question 8 why readers may consider this a valid pre-registration nevertheless.
table.research_questions:
What is the effect of a one-week social media abstinence (detox) on social media use (SMU), subjective automaticity of SMU and subjective craving for SMU? And do automaticity, craving and motivation to change SMU mediate the effect of detox on SMU? 

We hypothesize that participants’ social media use (H1) and subjective automaticity (H2) will be reduced after the detox, while subjective craving will increase during the detox (H3).
table.design_dependent_variables:
Social media usage
Participants will be asked once a week to enter objective smartphone usage statistics, as obtained from preinstalled smartphone apps ‘Screen Time’ (for iPhone) or ‘Digital Wellbeing’ (for Android). Participants will enter daily time spent on their top three social media applications, their daily total usage and the number of unlocks. 

Craving and automaticity 
These will be measured with single questions thrice daily using EMA and using more extensive questionnaires on a weekly basis.

Weekly measurements
-	Craving: measured using the 5-item Social Media Craving Scale (SMCS; Savci & Griffiths, 2019). 
-	Automaticity: measured using the 4-item Self-Report Behavioural Automaticity Index (SRBAI; Gardner et al., 2012), separately for opening and for using social media.

Ecological Momentary Assessments
The mobile app Ethica will be used to ask participants, thrice a day, to answer two questions on a 7-point VAS-scale: 
-	Craving: "How strong is your desire to go on social media in the last hour?”
-	Automaticity: “To what extent was checking your social media automatic?”. This question will only be presented in case participants indicate they have been on social media since the previous assessment.
-	During the detox, we will additionally ask participants once a day to report on the number of habitual ‘slips’, defined as the number of times they wanted to open a social media app before realising it was removed.
table.study_design_overview:
Participants will be randomly assigned to either the detox or waitlist condition. 
Detox condition: participants will start with one week of baseline (use as usual), followed by a week of detox and three weeks of post-detox measurements (total 5 weeks). 
Waitlist condition: participants will start with three weeks of baseline (use as usual), followed by a week of detox and three weeks of post-detox measurements (total 7 weeks).
Groups will be matched on age and gender (we will compare groups after reaching 40 inclusions / group).

During the week of detox, participants will be asked to remove all social media apps (defined for this study as: Facebook, YouTube, Instagram, Snapchat, Twitter, Pinterest, Tumblr, TikTok, Buzzfeed and Reddit) from their phone and log-out from and stop using these social media platforms on any other device. 

Inclusion criteria are: 
-	Aged between 16 and 40 years old
-	Spending >1 hour daily (self-reported) on social media platforms (Facebook, YouTube, Instagram, Snapchat, Twitter, Pinterest, Tumblr, TikTok, Buzzfeed and Reddit) prior to the study 
-	Motivated to reduce social media use
-	Willingness to stop using social media and remove social media apps from their smartphone during the detox
table.statistical_tests:
Weekly measurements
Mixed ANOVAs will be used to test each of the main hypotheses, using the weekly averages of SMU and the weekly measures of craving and automaticity as DVs and including within-subject factor time (pre/post-detox) and between-subject factor group (detox/waitlist control). We expect significant interactions between Time and Group, reflecting that the detox has a significant effect on these measures post- versus pre-detox in the detox compared to waitlist group.

Linear mixed modeling will be used to test if pre-post SMU change can be predicted based on self-reported craving during detox, pre-post changes in self-reported automaticity and motivation to change SMU. We expect smaller decreases in automaticity and bigger increases in craving to be predictive of detox success (in terms of the pre/post differences in SMU). We will additionally explore mediating effects of other factors such as motivation to reduce SMU and clinical and personality factors.
table.outliers_and_exclusions:
Participants who miss one of the weekly questionnaires will be excluded from the weekly analyses. 
Participants who miss two full consecutive days of EMA measurements will be excluded from the EMA analyses. 
Adherence to detox: In case participants spend >20% of baseline SMU during the detox, they will be excluded from the analyses. We will perform additional sensitivity analyses with and without participants who failed to be offline during the detox. 
During preliminary analysis, data will be examined for multivariate normality. If the data is not normally distributed, log transformations will be applied. If insufficient, non-parametric tests will be used.
table.sample_size: We aim to recruit a total of 100 usable datasets for the main analyses (related to the weekly measurements), evenly distributed over the two conditions.
table.additional_comments:
About data collection: The first batch of participants (n=14) started three days ago with their baseline measurement, but this study was preregistered before any participants started with the detox phase. This does not impact our hypotheses and analysis-plans described here in any way, so this should be considered as a valid pre-registration.

Secondary analyses: 
Participants will be invited to fill out follow-up questionnaires at 6-, 12- and 24-weeks post-detox (same measures as the weekly questionnaires) to test the long-term effects of the detox on SMU, automaticity, craving and motivation. 

We also aim to test if the number of self-reported habitual ‘slips’ during the detox week can be predicted based on the average baseline SMU, self-reported automaticity or craving. 

Exploratory analyses: 
Daily SMU and EMA data
Multilevel modelling will be used with SMU as dependent variable and craving, automaticity and motivation to reduce SMU as predictors. 
We will also explore whether increased craved during detox can be modeled to predict SMU post-detox (‘incubation’ of craving).

We will separately explore the effects of the detox on various aspects of mental wellbeing (see mental health outcomes below). We plan to use the results of these exploratory analyses to guide hypotheses in a follow-up confirmatory study. 

Mental health and social media use outcomes
Weekly measures will further include the Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Wellbeing Scale (WEMWBS; Stewart-Brown & Janmohamed, 2008), the Depression, Anxiety, Stress Scale - 21 (DASS-21; Henry & Crawford, 2005), Social Media Disorder Scale (SMDS; van den Eijnden et al., 2016), the Sleep Question Scale (SQS; Snyder, Cai, DeMuro, Morrison, & Ball, 2018), and various questions about the way participants use and experience using social media (e.g. pleasure, agency).

table.title: The effect of a Digital Detox on social media use, craving and automaticity - sample size update
table.description:
Change in sample size plan: 

Soon after starting data collection, we realized that the pre-registered sampled size plan (“we aim to recruit a total of 100 usable datasets for the main analyses (related to the weekly measurements), evenly distributed over the two conditions. “), would be difficult to realize. This is because we would have to wait until the last participant finished the full 5/7-week procedure before we know how many complete datasets we have, continue with a new batch, wait for 5/7 weeks, check again and so on, until we have a total of 100. This could potentially take very long which is suboptimal and due to time-restrictions this is not feasible.
Therefore, we have added the following to our sample size rule: “We aim for a total of 100 usable datasets for the main analyses (related to the weekly measurements), evenly distributed over the two conditions. We will stop including new participants after 120 participants have been enrolled AND completed the first three weekly questionnaires (i.e. the end-of-detox questionnaire for the experimental group; 2nd week of baseline for the waiting list group), based on an expected 15% drop-out after that point.

These will be measured with single questions thrice daily using EMA and using more extensive questionnaires on a weekly basis.

Weekly measurements
-\tCraving: measured using the 5-item Social Media Craving Scale (SMCS; Savci & Griffiths, 2019).
-\tAutomaticity: measured using the 4-item Self-Report Behavioural Automaticity Index (SRBAI; Gardner et al., 2012), separately for opening and for using social media.

Ecological Momentary Assessments
The mobile app Ethica will be used to ask participants, thrice a day, to answer two questions on a 7-point VAS-scale:
-\tCraving: \"How strong is your desire to go on social media in the last hour?”
-\tAutomaticity: “To what extent was checking your social media automatic?”. This question will only be presented in case participants indicate they have been on social media since the previous assessment.
-\tDuring the detox, we will additionally ask participants once a day to report on the number of habitual ‘slips’, defined as the number of times they wanted to open a social media app before realising it was removed.", "Participants will be randomly assigned to either the detox or waitlist condition.
Detox condition: participants will start with one week of baseline (use as usual), followed by a week of detox and three weeks of post-detox measurements (total 5 weeks).
Waitlist condition: participants will start with three weeks of baseline (use as usual), followed by a week of detox and three weeks of post-detox measurements (total 7 weeks).
Groups will be matched on age and gender (we will compare groups after reaching 40 inclusions / group).

During the week of detox, participants will be asked to remove all social media apps (defined for this study as: Facebook, YouTube, Instagram, Snapchat, Twitter, Pinterest, Tumblr, TikTok, Buzzfeed and Reddit) from their phone and log-out from and stop using these social media platforms on any other device.

Inclusion criteria are:
-\tAged between 16 and 40 years old
-\tSpending >1 hour daily (self-reported) on social media platforms (Facebook, YouTube, Instagram, Snapchat, Twitter, Pinterest, Tumblr, TikTok, Buzzfeed and Reddit) prior to the study
-\tMotivated to reduce social media use
-\tWillingness to stop using social media and remove social media apps from their smartphone during the detox", "Weekly measurements
Mixed ANOVAs will be used to test each of the main hypotheses, using the weekly averages of SMU and the weekly measures of craving and automaticity as DVs and including within-subject factor time (pre/post-detox) and between-subject factor group (detox/waitlist control). We expect significant interactions between Time and Group, reflecting that the detox has a significant effect on these measures post- versus pre-detox in the detox compared to waitlist group.

Linear mixed modeling will be used to test if pre-post SMU change can be predicted based on self-reported craving during detox, pre-post changes in self-reported automaticity and motivation to change SMU. We expect smaller decreases in automaticity and bigger increases in craving to be predictive of detox success (in terms of the pre/post differences in SMU). We will additionally explore mediating effects of other factors such as motivation to reduce SMU and clinical and personality factors.", "Participants who miss one of the weekly questionnaires will be excluded from the weekly analyses.
Participants who miss two full consecutive days of EMA measurements will be excluded from the EMA analyses.
Adherence to detox: In case participants spend >20% of baseline SMU during the detox, they will be excluded from the analyses. We will perform additional sensitivity analyses with and without participants who failed to be offline during the detox.
During preliminary analysis, data will be examined for multivariate normality. If the data is not normally distributed, log transformations will be applied. If insufficient, non-parametric tests will be used.", "We aim to recruit a total of 100 usable datasets for the main analyses (related to the weekly measurements), evenly distributed over the two conditions.", "About data collection: The first batch of participants (n=14) started three days ago with their baseline measurement, but this study was preregistered before any participants started with the detox phase. This does not impact our hypotheses and analysis-plans described here in any way, so this should be considered as a valid pre-registration.

Secondary analyses:
Participants will be invited to fill out follow-up questionnaires at 6-, 12- and 24-weeks post-detox (same measures as the weekly questionnaires) to test the long-term effects of the detox on SMU, automaticity, craving and motivation.

We also aim to test if the number of self-reported habitual ‘slips’ during the detox week can be predicted based on the average baseline SMU, self-reported automaticity or craving.

Exploratory analyses:
Daily SMU and EMA data
Multilevel modelling will be used with SMU as dependent variable and craving, automaticity and motivation to reduce SMU as predictors.
We will also explore whether increased craved during detox can be modeled to predict SMU post-detox (‘incubation’ of craving).

We will separately explore the effects of the detox on various aspects of mental wellbeing (see mental health outcomes below). We plan to use the results of these exploratory analyses to guide hypotheses in a follow-up confirmatory study.

Mental health and social media use outcomes
Weekly measures will further include the Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Wellbeing Scale (WEMWBS; Stewart-Brown & Janmohamed, 2008), the Depression, Anxiety, Stress Scale - 21 (DASS-21; Henry & Crawford, 2005), Social Media Disorder Scale (SMDS; van den Eijnden et al., 2016), the Sleep Question Scale (SQS; Snyder, Cai, DeMuro, Morrison, & Ball, 2018), and various questions about the way participants use and experience using social media (e.g. pleasure, agency).", "The effect of a Digital Detox on social media use, craving and automaticity", "Experiment", NA, "input"), "Preregistration 2" = c("Open-Ended Registration", "The effect of a Digital Detox on social media use, craving and automaticity - sample size update", "gepnk", "https://osf.io/gepnk", "2021-04-19T08:52:38.507672", "2026-09-16T18:14:12.700324", "2021-04-19T08:52:38.491757", "2022-05-30T00:00:00Z", "https://archive.org/details/osf-registrations-gepnk-v1", NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, "Change in sample size plan:

Soon after starting data collection, we realized that the pre-registered sampled size plan (“we aim to recruit a total of 100 usable datasets for the main analyses (related to the weekly measurements), evenly distributed over the two conditions. “), would be difficult to realize. This is because we would have to wait until the last participant finished the full 5/7-week procedure before we know how many complete datasets we have, continue with a new batch, wait for 5/7 weeks, check again and so on, until we have a total of 100. This could potentially take very long which is suboptimal and due to time-restrictions this is not feasible.
Therefore, we have added the following to our sample size rule: “We aim for a total of 100 usable datasets for the main analyses (related to the weekly measurements), evenly distributed over the two conditions. We will stop including new participants after 120 participants have been enrolled AND completed the first three weekly questionnaires (i.e. the end-of-detox questionnaire for the experimental group; 2nd week of baseline for the waiting list group), based on an expected 15% drop-out after that point.", "input")), row.names = c("template_name", "title", "id", "link", "date_created", "date_modified", "date_registered", "embargo_end_date", "ia_url", "data_collection_started", "research_questions", "design_dependent_variables", "study_design_overview", "statistical_tests", "outliers_and_exclusions", "sample_size", "additional_comments", "name", "finally", "description", "paper_id"), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 5, FALSE) ``` ::: ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of deviations from preregistrations, see: van den Akker O, Bakker M, van Assen M, Pennington C, Verweij L, Elsherif M, Claesen A, Gaillard S, Yeung S, Frankenberger J, Krautter K, Cockcroft J, Kreuer K, Evans T, Heppel F, Schoch S, Korbmacher M, Yamada Y, Albayrak-Aydemir N, Wicherts J (2024). “The potential of preregistration in psychology: Assessing preregistration producibility and preregistration-study consistency.” Psychological Methods. doi:10.1037/met0000687. table.header: 3.3.9 Effect of detox on affective and mental wellbeing
table.expanded: Mental wellbeing significantly improved during the detox week (d = 0.42), and sleep quality showed a small, non-significant improvement (d = 0.23, 95% CI [0.04, 0.42]; p = .057 after Bonferroni correction).

table.formatted: Moreover, the time course of mental wellbeing, anxiety and stress differed between groups (Group × Time, all ps ≤ .037; Supplementary Table <ref type="table">S6</ref>): both groups improved during their detox, but only the immediatedetox group maintained these improvements afterwards, whereas the waitlist group returned to baseline.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("ps ≥ .16", "ps > .51", "ps > .32", 
"ps > .41", "ps ≤ .041", "ps ≤ .037", "ps > .50", "ps < .005", 
"ps ≤ .001", "ps ≤ .005"), Text = c("The groups did not differ significantly on age, gender, education, or smartphone related metrics (all ps ≥ .16; see Table 2) indicating that randomization was successful.", 
"Responders and non-responders did not differ in pre-post SMU change (both ps > .51), nor in baseline or post-detox SMU (all ps > .32) at either follow-up, indicating that the long-term reductions were not driven by differential retention of stronger responders.", 
"Responders and non-responders did not differ in pre-post SMU change (both ps > .51), nor in baseline or post-detox SMU (all ps > .32) at either follow-up, indicating that the long-term reductions were not driven by differential retention of stronger responders.", 
"After the detox, total screentime was still lower than baseline one week post-detox (p = .002), in line with the sustained reduction in SMU, and returned to baseline by three weeks (p = .24), whereas nonsocial-media screentime returned to baseline at both timepoints (both ps > .41).", 
"All five measures showed a significant main effect of Time (all ps ≤ .041; Figure 5 and Supplementary Table S6), driven by two different patterns of results.", 
"Moreover, the time course of mental wellbeing, anxiety and stress differed between groups (Group × Time, all ps ≤ .037; Supplementary Table S6): both groups improved during their detox, but only the immediatedetox group maintained these improvements afterwards, whereas the waitlist group returned to baseline.", 
"Baseline social media use and screen time did not differ (ps > .50).", 
"However, including the three participants this affected did not change the main between-group results (Group × Time: SMU F(1, 118) = 19.28, automaticity F(1, 118) = 34.36, craving F(1, 118) = 8.25, all ps < .005).", 
"Log-transformed SMU (log[x + 1], as some values were zero) gave the same results for the between-group effect, the within-subject effect of Time up to three weeks post-detox, the 12-and 24-week comparisons with baseline, and RQ4 (all ps ≤ .001, except 12 weeks vs.", 
"The 12-and 24-week comparisons also held in Wilcoxon signed-rank tests (ps ≤ .005)."
)), row.names = c(NA, -10L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

table.header: 3.1 Sample characteristics & randomization check
table.expanded: The groups did not differ significantly on age, gender, education, or smartphone related metrics (all ps ≥ .16; see Table 2) indicating that randomization was successful.

table.formatted: The detox was effective at reducing usage: participants in the detox group reduced their daily social media use by ~41 minutes (38.1%), from M = 107.2 minutes (SD = 61.0) at baseline to M = 66.4 minutes (SD = 58.0) one week post-detox (t(115) = 5.82, p < .001), whereas the waitlist group showed no meaningful change (M = 113.7, SD = 67.1 to M = 112.2 minutes, SD = 75.1; t(115) = 0.24, p = .81).
table.header: 3.2.1 RQ1: what is the effect of the detox on social media use?
table.expanded: The detox was effective at reducing usage: participants in the detox group reduced their daily social media use by ~41 minutes (38.1%), from M = 107.2 minutes (SD = 61.0) at baseline to M = 66.4 minutes (SD = 58.0) one week post-detox (t(115) = 5.82, p < .001), whereas the waitlist group showed no meaningful change (M = 113.7, SD = 67.1 to M = 112.2 minutes, SD = 75.1; t(115) = 0.24, p = .81).

table.formatted: Subjective automaticity (range 1-7) was high at baseline in both the detox group (M = 5.52, SD = .94) and the waitlist group (M = 5.59, SD = .95), and significantly reduced one week post-detox in the detox group (M = 4.32, SD = 1.59; t(115) = 7.28, p < .001) but not the waitlist group (M = 5.62, SD = 1.06; t(115) = -0.18, p = .85).
table.header: 3.2.2 RQ2: what is the effect of the detox on subjective automaticity?
table.expanded: Subjective automaticity (range 1-7) was high at baseline in both the detox group (M = 5.52, SD = .94) and the waitlist group (M = 5.59, SD = .95), and significantly reduced one week post-detox in the detox group (M = 4.32, SD = 1.59; t(115) = 7.28, p < .001) but not the waitlist group (M = 5.62, SD = 1.06; t(115) = -0.18, p = .85).

table.formatted: A significant main effect of Time, F(1, 115) = 17.73, p < .001, η²p = .13, but not Group, F(1, 115) = 0.82, p = .37, η²p = .01, was further explained by a Group × Time interaction, F(1, 115) = 7.73, p = .006, η²p = .06.
table.header: 3.2.3 RQ3: what is the effect of the detox on craving?
table.expanded: A significant main effect of Time, F(1, 115) = 17.73, p < .001, η²p = .13, but not Group, F(1, 115) = 0.82, p = .37, η²p = .01, was further explained by a Group × Time interaction, F(1, 115) = 7.73, p = .006, η²p = .06.

table.formatted: This effect was driven by a significant decrease in craving in the detox group (from M = 2.82, SD = 1.02 at baseline to M = 2.23, SD = .96 post-detox; t(115) = 4.62, p < .001), which was absent in the waitlist group (from M = 2.73, SD = 0.98 to M = 2.61, SD = 0.98; t(115) = 1.09, p = .28).
table.header: 3.2.3 RQ3: what is the effect of the detox on craving?

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. stat_effect_size.summary_text: We found 15 t-tests and/or F-tests where effect sizes are not reported. Check these tests in the table below, and consider adding effect sizes.

info.title: Disrupting social media habits: a one-week detox produces enduring reductions in use and automaticity

text.text: This randomised controlled trial examines if a one-week social media abstinence intervention can reduce social media use by lowering automaticity of and craving for social media use.
Participants motivated to reduce their social media use were assigned to an immediate one-week detox (N = 50) or a waitlist control condition (N = 67).

Using a combination of smartphone usage logging and weekly surveys, we found that the detox produced significant reductions in social media use (d = 0.79), automaticity (d = 1.05), and craving (d = 0.52) one week post-detox relative to the waitlist group.

Pooling data from both groups after each had completed the detox (N = 112), we found that larger reductions in automaticity predicted larger reductions in use, and that baseline automaticity predicted self-reported attempts to open removed apps (i.e. habitual slips of action) during the detox.
The reductions persisted across the three-week followup, and social media use remained below baseline at a six-month follow-up in a subsample (N = 49).

The detox also shifted participants' subjective relationship with social media, increasing perceived control and reducing self-reported mindlessness, without changing how much they liked it or considered it purposeful.
Together, these findings suggest that, for those who want to cut back, taking a short break is an effective way to disrupt social media habits and restore a sense of control.
Social media has become a central part of daily life.
Worldwide, almost 6 billion people (around 2 in 3) spend on average more than 18 hours weekly on those platforms (Global Social Media Statistics, 2026).
text.formatted: Worldwide, almost 6 billion people (around 2 in 3) spend on average more than 18 hours weekly on those platforms <ref type="bibr">(Global Social Media Statistics, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: This popularity makes sense: social media serves many genuine needs, from staying connected and informed to entertainment and self-expression (Whiting & Williams, 2013).
text.formatted: This popularity makes sense: social media serves many genuine needs, from staying connected and informed to entertainment and self-expression <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Whiting & Williams, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: At the same time, most people spend more time on social media than they want to, and struggle to cut back (Dekker et al., 2026).
text.formatted: At the same time, most people spend more time on social media than they want to, and struggle to cut back <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Dekker et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The tension between the value social media offers and the difficulty of using it in a balanced way sits at the heart of growing concerns about digital wellbeing (Vanden Abeele, 2020).
text.formatted: The tension between the value social media offers and the difficulty of using it in a balanced way sits at the heart of growing concerns about digital wellbeing <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Vanden Abeele, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Why is it so hard to strike this balance, and can a temporary break from social media help restore it?
In this study, we investigate whether a one-week social media detox produces lasting reductions in social media use, and whether it does so by disrupting the habits that normally drive use.
People often fail to change their behaviour despite good intentions, a phenomenon known as the intention-behaviour gap (Sheeran & Webb, 2016).
text.formatted: People often fail to change their behaviour despite good intentions, a phenomenon known as the intention-behaviour gap <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Sheeran & Webb, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: A key reason is that much of our behaviour is not deliberately controlled but habitual.
Habits are automatic, cue-triggered behaviours that operate largely independently of current goals (Wood & Rünger, 2016).
text.formatted: Habits are automatic, cue-triggered behaviours that operate largely independently of current goals <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Wood & Rünger, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: These features make habits hard to change: because they are triggered by context rather than intention, they can persist even when they conflict with what we want.
Habits form when a behaviour is repeated frequently in a stable context -and few behaviours are repeated as frequently, in as many contexts, as social media use.
This makes social media use a strong candidate for being highly habitual (Anderson & Wood, 2025; Bayer et al., 2022).
text.formatted: This makes social media use a strong candidate for being highly habitual <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Anderson & Wood, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Bayer et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, early research found that smartphone checking habits -brief, automatic inspections of the phone -characterize smartphone use (Oulasvirta et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Indeed, early research found that smartphone checking habits -brief, automatic inspections of the phone -characterize smartphone use <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Oulasvirta et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: In line with the idea that habits undermine intentions, people who report stronger social media checking habits also report more difficulty controlling their use (Du et al., 2019).
text.formatted: In line with the idea that habits undermine intentions, people who report stronger social media checking habits also report more difficulty controlling their use <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Du et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: One increasingly popular way to regain control is a period of abstinence, or 'digital detox' (Nguyen, 2021; Radtke et al., 2021).
text.formatted: One increasingly popular way to regain control is a period of abstinence, or 'digital detox' <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Nguyen, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Radtke et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The central assumption is that a digital detox can help people break their unwanted social media habits.
This effect may be achieved by removing behavioural accessibility -one of several strategies for disrupting habitual behaviour (Gardner et al., 2024; Wood & Neal, 2016).
text.formatted: This effect may be achieved by removing behavioural accessibility -one of several strategies for disrupting habitual behaviour <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Gardner et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Wood & Neal, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: By removing social media apps from one's phone, a detox makes the habitual response temporarily unavailable, creating a 'window of opportunity' to shift toward alternative behaviours (Gardner et al., 2024; Verplanken et al., 2018).
text.formatted: By removing social media apps from one's phone, a detox makes the habitual response temporarily unavailable, creating a 'window of opportunity' to shift toward alternative behaviours <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Gardner et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Verplanken et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Because the habitual response repeatedly goes unperformed, the underlying cue-response association may weaken (or be overridden by alternative cue-response associations).

We therefore expect more sustained reductions in use for those in whom the detox more strongly reduces the subjective automaticity of their social media use -a proxy for habit strength (Gardner et al., 2012).
text.formatted: We therefore expect more sustained reductions in use for those in whom the detox more strongly reduces the subjective automaticity of their social media use -a proxy for habit strength <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Gardner et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Restricting behavioural accessibility, however, may have a downside.
Blocking the response while the triggers for use remain may increase the urge to use.
Such an 'incubation of craving' is well-documented across substance use disorders (e.g. Bedi et al., 2011; Li et al., 2014), and behavioural addictions (Fernandez et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Such an 'incubation of craving' is well-documented across substance use disorders (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Bedi et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Li et al., 2014)</ref>, and behavioural addictions <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Fernandez et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, previous studies have observed increased social media craving during (Wadsley & Ihssen, 2023; Wilcockson et al., 2019) and following (Stieger & Lewetz, 2018) a detox, raising the possibility that craving leads to a rebound effect once the apps are again available.
text.formatted: Similarly, previous studies have observed increased social media craving during <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Wadsley & Ihssen, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Wilcockson et al., 2019)</ref> and following <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Stieger & Lewetz, 2018)</ref> a detox, raising the possibility that craving leads to a rebound effect once the apps are again available.

text.text: In the current study, we therefore assess both habit as a potential mechanism of the detox's effect, and craving as a process that may work against it.
Taken together, these observations highlight two research gaps.

First, it remains largely unknown whether a detox produces reductions in use that persist after normal access resumes, because most studies measure effects only during the abstinence period itself (Radtke et al., 2021).
text.formatted: First, it remains largely unknown whether a detox produces reductions in use that persist after normal access resumes, because most studies measure effects only during the abstinence period itself <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Radtke et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Second, to the extent that a detox does reduce subsequent use, the question remains through which mechanisms it does so.

In the present study, to address both gaps, we invited participants motivated to reduce their social media use to complete a one-week social media detox, and followed them for three weeks after the detox, and a subset for even longer (six months).

Using a randomised controlled trial combined with a longitudinal within-subject design, participants were randomly assigned to detox either immediately or after a three-week waiting period (waitlist control), with weekly surveys throughout.
The randomised comparison allowed us to causally test the detox's effects up to one week post-detox, after which the waitlist group underwent the detox as well.
Pooling both groups after each had detoxed additionally allowed us to test the persistence of the effect within-subject in the full sample.

Objectively logged social media use, self-reported automaticity, and craving were measured at baseline and across the three-week follow-up, alongside participants' subjective experience of their social media use and mental wellbeing.
Our preregistered research questions were: (1) does a one-week detox reduce social media use; (2) does it reduce automaticity of social media use; (3) does it affect craving.
text.formatted: Our preregistered research questions were: (1) does a one-week detox reduce social media use; <ref type="bibr">(2)</ref> does it reduce automaticity of social media use; (3) does it affect craving.

text.text: We hypothesised that social media use and automaticity would be reduced after the detox, while craving would increase during it.

We further preregistered to test if (4) changes in automaticity, craving, and baseline motivation predict the reduction in social media use, and (5) baseline social media use, automaticity, or craving predict the number of times during the detox participants reported wanting to open the app before realising it was removed (i.e. slip of action).
Exploratory analyses were run on the effect of the detox on social media and general smartphone use, the subjective experience of social media use, and mental and affective wellbeing.
These exploratory analyses used within-subject comparisons (baseline to postdetox), allowing us to examine effects up to three weeks following the detox.

The present study was pre-registered on the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/9k8rw/), approved by the Psychology ethics committee of the University of Amsterdam (2020-CP-12644) and performed in accordance with those guidelines.
text.formatted: The present study was pre-registered on the Open Science Framework (<ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/9k8rw/">https://osf.io/9k8rw/</ref>), approved by the Psychology ethics committee of the University of Amsterdam (2020-CP-12644) and performed in accordance with those guidelines.

text.text: Data collection took place between April and July 2021.
Participants were recruited through the university network and paid advertisements on Facebook and Instagram.
Before admission, participants signed an informed consent form and completed an inclusion screener.
Criteria were: age 16-40, EU residence, Android or iOS phone ownership, daily social media use of at least one hour, and motivation and willingness to remove their social media apps for one week.

We selected highly motivated participants to match the target group for whom a detox is a plausible intervention, and to avoid known problems with unmotivated participants such as non-adherence, dropout and negative wellbeing effects (Vanden Abeele et al., 2025).
text.formatted: We selected highly motivated participants to match the target group for whom a detox is a plausible intervention, and to avoid known problems with unmotivated participants such as non-adherence, dropout and negative wellbeing effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Vanden Abeele et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The study was conducted in both English (n = 49) and Dutch (n = 68), with participants completing all materials in their chosen language.
Participants received €25 for completing the study.
We deliberately kept the compensation relatively modest, to select for participants who were intrinsically motivated to detox.
Additionally, participants could win €5 per day through a lottery draw tied to EMA compliance, where each completed survey (three per day) served as a lottery ticket.
Any bonus earnings were paid out at the end of the study.
The original preregistration specified a target of 100 usable datasets, evenly distributed across conditions.

Shortly after data collection began, we updated the stopping rule via a registered amendment (https://osf.io/gepnk/),, as recruiting in discrete batches and waiting up to seven weeks per batch to assess attrition made the original plan logistically unfeasible within the available timeframe.
text.formatted: Shortly after data collection began, we updated the stopping rule via a registered amendment (<ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/gepnk/">https://osf.io/gepnk/</ref>),, as recruiting in discrete batches and waiting up to seven weeks per batch to assess attrition made the original plan logistically unfeasible within the available timeframe.

text.text: This amended stopping rule described that enrolment would cease after 120 participants had completed the first three weekly questionnaires, based on an expected 15% attrition rate thereafter.
Of the 233 eligible applicants, 76 (32%) dropped out before the study began, leaving 157 who started.
Of these, 30 (19%) did not complete the full three weeks and were excluded, leaving 127 completers.

This number is slightly higher than the target of 120 because some participants were already partway through the study when the enrolment threshold was reached, consistent with the anticipated attrition buffer.

Of the 127 completers, 10 were excluded for the following reasons: missing SMU data (n = 2), implausible smartphone data (weekly mean screen time below 15 min/day or above 16 h/day; n = 3), failing both attention checks (n = 1), and continued social media use during the detox exceeding the preregistered threshold of 20% of baseline usage (n = 4).
The final sample consisted of 117 participants.
A further exclusion based on the same detox-adherence threshold was applied to the waitlist group for the withinsubject analyses, resulting in N = 112 for those analyses.
This study employed a randomised controlled trial (RCT) design.
Participants were randomly assigned to either an immediate detox group or a waitlist group.

As illustrated in Figure 1, the waitlist group completed three weeks of baseline measurements before starting the detox, allowing us to compare detox and follow-up effects in the experimental group against the waitlist group's baseline weeks.
text.formatted: As illustrated in Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>, the waitlist group completed three weeks of baseline measurements before starting the detox, allowing us to compare detox and follow-up effects in the experimental group against the waitlist group's baseline weeks.

text.text: All participants ultimately completed the detox, enabling both a between-subjects comparison (n = 50 vs n = 67) and a within-subject analysis in a larger sample (n = 112).
Data were collected at four timepoints: baseline (T0), intervention (T1), post-detox (T2), and a final follow-up three weeks after the detox (T3).
The waitlist group had two additional baseline weeks before following the same procedure (BL0 and BL1), while BL2 did double duty as baseline (T0) for the within-subject comparisons.
During baseline week(s), participants were instructed to use social media as usual.
At the start of the detox week, they were asked to remove all social media apps from their smartphones and to stop using these platforms on any other devices or browsers (e.g., laptops, tablets).
The detox covered the following social media platforms: Facebook, Instagram, Pinterest, Reddit, Snapchat, TikTok, Buzzfeed, Tumblr, Twitter, and YouTube (selected based on Brown & Kuss, 2020).
text.formatted: The detox covered the following social media platforms: Facebook, Instagram, Pinterest, Reddit, Snapchat, TikTok, Buzzfeed, Tumblr, Twitter, and YouTube (selected based on <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Brown & Kuss, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: WhatsApp and similar direct-messaging apps were excluded, both because they fall outside the scope of social media as operationalised in the literature (Bayer et al., 2020) and for practical reasons.
text.formatted: WhatsApp and similar direct-messaging apps were excluded, both because they fall outside the scope of social media as operationalised in the literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bayer et al., 2020)</ref> and for practical reasons.

text.text: Participants were free to remove additional apps if they wished.
During the three follow-up weeks, participants could reinstall and use social media as they pleased.
Qualtrics survey (version April 2021), sent via an automated in-house mailing system.
A reminder was sent at 8pm if the survey had not yet been completed.
If participants had still not responded by the following morning, they were contacted by phone.
Those who had not completed the survey within 24 hours of the initial email (Tuesday noon) were dropped from the study.
Two attention checks were included at T1 and T2 (e.g., "If you are still paying attention, select 'Completely agree'").
One participant who failed both checks was excluded from the analyses.
To enhance detox compliance, we implemented several behaviour change techniques at the start of the intervention.
These included signing a self-commitment contract and watching a motivational video.
Participants also reflected on their reasons and goals for the detox, anticipated challenges, and strategies to overcome them.

Social media use was measured throughout the study period, and automaticity of social media use and craving for social media were measured (for each preceding week) at T0-T3 in the experimental group, and additionally at BL0-BL2 in the waitlist group.
Additional survey variables are described in the main text.
The measures described below were administered at all timepoints, with the exception of BL1 for the waitlist group, where the craving and mental wellbeing surveys were unintentionally omitted.

This precluded a between-groups test of changes during the detox week for these measures, but the pre-post comparisons (comparing T0 and T2 to BL0 and BL2, respectively) and within-detox-group changes (T0 vs.

text.text: T1) were unaffected.
In all surveys, participants were asked to reflect on their experience over the past week.
Social media and smartphone usage were assessed using the built-in smartphone apps Screen Time (iOS) and Digital Wellbeing (Android).

At each timepoint, participants retrieved and reported three metrics from the preceding week: (1) total daily screen time, (2) daily number of unlocks (referred to throughout as "pickups"), and (3) (time spent on) top three most-used social media apps, which we subsequently summed to obtain daily social media use.
Weekly scores were computed as the average of the available daily values.
At T0 and T3, participants retrospectively reported the preceding two weeks.
At the end of the detox week, participants additionally uploaded screenshots of their Screen Time or Digital Wellbeing data.
These were requested to encourage accurate self-report, and only in case of doubt did we cross-reference them with the reported values.
The processing of the reported values is described in the Supplementary Methods.
Because iOS and Android operationalise these metrics slightly differently, we compared baseline values between operating systems.
Only pickups differed (Supplementary Methods).
Because pickups were only analysed as within-person change over time, we pooled across both operating systems in all analyses.

Subjective automaticity was measured using the Self-Report Behavioural Automaticity Index (SRBAI; Gardner et al., 2012), a four-item scale (e.g., "I do automatically," "I do without thinking") with responses ranging from 'Strongly disagree' (1) to 'Strongly agree' (7).
text.formatted: Subjective automaticity was measured using the Self-Report Behavioural Automaticity Index (SRBAI; <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Gardner et al., 2012)</ref>, a four-item scale (e.g., "I do automatically," "I do without thinking") with responses ranging from 'Strongly disagree' (1) to 'Strongly agree' (7).

text.text: Participants completed the SRBAI only if they reported using social media in the past week.

Following our preregistration, we distinguished between automaticity of opening (reflecting on the moment of selecting a social media app) and automaticity of usage (reflecting on scrolling behaviour once the app is open), using the stem "Going on social media is something…" and "Using social media (i.e., once opened and scrolling) is something…," respectively.
Scores were computed as the mean across four items (range 1-7).
Reliability was excellent across timepoints (Cronbach's α = .87-.94).
The two scales were highly correlated across timepoints (r = .67-.78; Supplementary Table S8), indicating substantial shared variance.
text.formatted: The two scales were highly correlated across timepoints (r = .67-.78; Supplementary Table <ref type="table">S8</ref>), indicating substantial shared variance.

text.text: Since the intervention primarily targets the initiation of social media use, all analyses focus on automaticity of opening.
The detox effect was also present for automaticity of usage (Group × Time, F(1, 115) = 17.67, p < .001).
text.formatted: The detox effect was also present for automaticity of usage (Group × Time, F(1, 115) = 17.67, p < .001).

text.text: Craving was measured using the five-item Social Media Craving Scale (SMCS; Savci & Griffiths, 2019).
text.formatted: Craving was measured using the five-item Social Media Craving Scale (SMCS; <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Savci & Griffiths, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Items assess the frequency, intensity, and duration of craving, ability to resist craving, and overall craving severity, rated on a 7-point scale (0-6).
An example item is: "In the past week, how often have you thought about using social media, or about how good using social media would make you feel?"
The scale score is the mean of all five items (range 0-6), with higher scores indicating greater craving.
Reliability was good across timepoints (Cronbach's α = .79-.86).

To examine whether participants continued to reach for social media apps after removing them -i.e. habitual 'slips' -we asked, each evening during the detox: "Did you have a moment today that you wanted to open one of your social media apps, before realizing that the app had been removed from your phone?"
Those who responded positively were asked to estimate how often using ordinal categories (1 = 1-3 times,2 = 4-6 times,3 = 7-10 times,4 = 10+ times).
These data were collected using the Avicenna mobile application (Avicenna Research, https://avicennaresearch.com/ formerly Ethica Data).
text.formatted: These data were collected using the Avicenna mobile application (Avicenna Research, <ref type="url" target="https://avicennaresearch.com/">avicennaresearch.com,</ref> formerly Ethica Data).

text.text: Throughout the whole study, participants also completed brief Ecological Momentary Assessment (EMA) surveys on craving and automaticity three times daily (at pseudo-randomised times within fixed morning, afternoon, and evening windows).
This repeated self-monitoring likely encouraged active reflection, which we expected to improve the accuracy of weekly retrospective assessments.
Participants completed three self-report measures related to their psychological functioning at each survey timepoint.

Mental wellbeing was assessed with the Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Wellbeing Scale (WEMWBS; (Tennant et al., 2007), a 14-item measure of positive aspects of mental wellbeing covering psychological functioning, satisfying interpersonal relationships, and positive affect.
text.formatted: Mental wellbeing was assessed with the Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Wellbeing Scale (WEMWBS; <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Tennant et al., 2007)</ref>, a 14-item measure of positive aspects of mental wellbeing covering psychological functioning, satisfying interpersonal relationships, and positive affect.

text.text: Items are rated on a 5-point Likert scale (1 = none of the time to5 = all the time) and summed to a total score ranging from 14 to 70.
Higher scores indicate greater mental wellbeing.
Sleep quality was measured with the single-item Sleep Quality Scale (Snyder et al., 2018), in which participants rated their sleep over the past week from0 = terrible to10 = excellent.
text.formatted: Sleep quality was measured with the single-item Sleep Quality Scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Snyder et al., 2018)</ref>, in which participants rated their sleep over the past week from0 = terrible to10 = excellent.

text.text: Symptoms of depression, anxiety, and stress were assessed with the 21-item Depression Anxiety Stress Scales (DASS-21; Henry & Crawford, 2005), which contains three subscales of 7 items each.
text.formatted: Symptoms of depression, anxiety, and stress were assessed with the 21-item Depression Anxiety Stress Scales (DASS-21; <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Henry & Crawford, 2005)</ref>, which contains three subscales of 7 items each.

text.text: Items are rated on a 4-point scale (0 = not at all to3 = very much) and summed within each subscale.
Subscale scores are multiplied by two following standard scoring conventions, yielding a range of 0-42 per subscale with higher scores indicating greater symptom severity.
Internal consistency across the four timepoints was good to excellent for all scales: WEMWBS α = .90 -.94, DASS-21 anxiety α = .76 -.85, depression α = .86 -.90, and stress α = .81 -.85.
As preregistered, participants were invited to complete follow-up surveys post-detox, including the same questionnaires as the weekly surveys (with weekly rather than daily screentime metrics).
The 12-week follow-up offered €5 compensation and yielded a low response rate (n = 34).

To improve response for the final follow-up, we increased compensation to €10 and sent reminder emails, resulting in a higher response rate at 24 weeks (n = 51, of whom 49 provided usable objective social media use data).

Because the 24-week wave yielded a substantially larger sample than the 12-week wave, we report self-report measures from the 24-week followup in the main text (12-week results in Supplementary Table S4), whereas for social media use, our primary outcome, we report both follow-ups.

text.text: At baseline (T0), participants completed a survey that included questions on demographics (gender, age, education, employment), and open-ended questions about how they used social media.

Both before and after the detox, participants reported on their subjective experiences with using social media, including perceived control over use, purposefulness of use, proportion of mindless use, perceived appropriateness of one's SMU, and liking of social media (details are in Supplementary Table S2).
text.formatted: Both before and after the detox, participants reported on their subjective experiences with using social media, including perceived control over use, purposefulness of use, proportion of mindless use, perceived appropriateness of one's SMU, and liking of social media (details are in Supplementary Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S2</ref>).

text.text: At the end of the detox (T1i and T3w), we additionally inquired about their experiences with the detox.

This included questions about whether they found the detox useful (1 = not useful,7 = extremely useful), if they would recommend the detox, and if they became aware of any triggers of social media use.
Below, we describe our preregistered confirmatory analyses followed by exploratory analyses.
Across these analyses, two complementary analytical approaches were used.

The first approach is a between-groups comparison of the immediate detox (N = 50) and waitlist group (N = 67), used for the three preregistered hypotheses on the effect of the detox (RQ1-RQ3), and the exploratory mediation and moderation analyses.

The second approach combines data from both groups after each had completed the detox, providing within-subject pre-post comparisons for the full sample (N = 112) across up to three weeks of follow-up.

This was used for the two remaining preregistered analyses regarding predictors of the reduction in SMU (RQ4) and habitual slips during the detox (RQ5), and for the exploratory analyses on longitudinal effects and mental wellbeing.
Analyses were conducted in R, version 4.5.3 (R Core Team, 2026).
We first describe the confirmatory analyses corresponding to our five preregistered research questions.
Deviations from the preregistration are reported under 2.5.

Three confirmatory hypotheses concerning the effects of the detox on social media use (RQ1), automaticity (RQ2), and craving (RQ3) were tested using mixed ANOVAs with Time (pre, post) as a within-subject factor and Group (detox, waitlist) as a between-subjects factor.
For SMU, baseline was computed as the average of the two weeks preceding the detox to obtain a stable estimate, given that daily SMU can fluctuate considerably.
For automaticity and craving, the single pre-detox baseline week was used (a two-week automaticity baseline, as in the within-subject analyses, gave the same result; Supplementary Section S3.5).
A significant Group × Time interaction would reflect a differential pre-to post-detox change between groups.

Significant interactions were followed by planned simple effects (pre vs. post within each group), reported without correction for multiple comparisons given the small number of a priori, directional contrasts.

As robustness checks on the preregistered between-groups results, we additionally report (a) the SMU analysis excluding extreme outliers (defined as values > 3 SD from the within-group mean on the post-detox measure) and (b) comparisons of pre-post change scores between groups with an independent t-test, which also provided Cohen's d with 95% confidence intervals.
text.formatted: As robustness checks on the preregistered between-groups results, we additionally report (a) the SMU analysis excluding extreme outliers (defined as values > 3 SD from the within-group mean on the post-detox measure) and (b) comparisons of pre-post change scores between groups with an independent t-test, which also provided Cohen's d with 95% confidence intervals.

text.text: As preregistered, we also repeated the analyses including the participants who did not adhere to the detox, restricted to participants who did not use social media at all during the detox, with log-transformed SMU, and with non-parametric tests (Supplementary Section S3.5).
RQ4 tested whether the reduction in SMU following the detox could be predicted by (i) prepost change in automaticity, (ii) during-detox craving, and (iii) baseline motivation to reduce SMU.
We tested this with a multiple regression of pre-post SMU change on the three predictors (preregistered as a linear mixed model; Supplementary Materials S2, Deviation 3).
We additionally report an ANCOVA predicting post-detox SMU from baseline SMU and the same predictors, which adjusts for individual differences in starting level.
The preregistered research question was whether automaticity, craving and motivation mediate the effect of the detox on SMU.
We therefore additionally report formal mediation analyses (Section 3.3.1) as a more direct (but exploratory) test of the mediation hypothesis.
For RQ5, we tested the preregistered prediction that the number of habitual slips during the detox week could be predicted from baseline SMU, automaticity, and craving.
Two participants did not complete the daily slips reports, so this analysis included 110 participants.
As for SMU, baseline automaticity in the within-subject analyses was the mean of the two predetox weeks, to obtain a more reliable baseline for the change scores.
Craving was only measured in the last pre-detox week.
The ordinal frequency categories were recoded to approximate counts (Supplementary Materials, Section S1.3), and the seven daily values were averaged into a weekly mean slips score.
We tested the preregistered hypothesis by entering baseline SMU, automaticity, and craving simultaneously as predictors in a regression model on the weekly mean.

As a robustness check, given the right-skewed count nature of the slips outcome, we repeated the regression as a negative binomial model of the weekly total of the recoded daily values, with the number of completed daily reports as offset.

We additionally examined how slips developed over the course of the detox week with an exploratory repeatedmeasures ANOVA on the seven daily values, restricted to the 81 participants who completed all seven daily reports.
We conducted several exploratory analyses to complement the preregistered tests.

Using the between-group sample, we tested whether the detox's effect on SMU was mediated by changes in automaticity or craving, and whether baseline characteristics moderated the effect (3.3.1-3.3.2).
Using the within-subject sample, we examined how a range of outcomes changed over time with mixed ANOVAs, including Time as a within-subject factor.
The specific timepoints varied by measure and are stated with each result.

Group (initial detox vs. initial waitlist) was added as a between-subject factor to check whether within-subject trajectories differed between the groups; all Group and Group × Time effects are reported in the Supplementary Material (Section S3.6 and Tables S5 and S6).
text.formatted: Group (initial detox vs. initial waitlist) was added as a between-subject factor to check whether within-subject trajectories differed between the groups; all Group and Group × Time effects are reported in the Supplementary Material (Section S3.6 and Tables <ref type="table">S5</ref> and <ref type="table">S6</ref>).

text.text: Post-hoc comparisons were Bonferroni-corrected.
We deviated from the preregistration on nine points (Supplementary Section S2).
One affects the interpretation of a confirmatory result: H3 predicted that craving would increase during the detox, but the analysis plan specified only a pre/post-detox comparison.
We therefore tested H3 within participants (Section 3.3.5), which is a less severe test than a between-group comparison.
The other deviations concern a reversed expected direction in the RQ4 analysis plan, analytic details the preregistration did not specify, and the missing 6-week follow-up.

text.text: The 117 included participants were randomly assigned to the detox group (n = 50) or a waitlist group (n = 67).
The sample was predominantly female (106 female, 10 male, 1 other) and highly educated, with an average age of 23.5 years (SD = 4.0; range 17-37; one participant did not report their age).
Of the 117 participants, 72 (62%) used iPhones and 45 (38%) used Android devices.
The groups did not differ significantly on age, gender, education, or smartphone related metrics (all ps ≥ .16; see Table 2) indicating that randomization was successful.
text.formatted: The groups did not differ significantly on age, gender, education, or smartphone related metrics (all ps ≥ .16; see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">2</ref>) indicating that randomization was successful.

text.text: Instagram was indicated most as primary social media app (n = 64, 54.7% of participants), while Facebook (n = 15, 12.8%), TikTok (n = 15, 12.8%) and YouTube (n = 15, 12.8%) were also often listed.

As main reasons for the detox, participants selected most frequently: "Reduce my social media use, in order to free up time for other activities" (n = 87, 74.4%) and "Experience how it is to be offline, to get insight" (n = 76, 65.0%).
On average, participants rated the detox as useful (M = 4.89, SD = 1.14 on a 1-7 scale) and 93% would recommend the detox to a friend.
When asked whether they had become aware of triggers that would normally initiate their social media use, the large majority of participants (90%) answered yes and elaborated on specific cues.
By far the most frequently mentioned trigger was boredom (63% of elaborated responses).

Another set of triggers clustered around downtime and transitional moments: breaks from work or study (26%), waiting or commuting (21%), idle time (11%), and moments around waking or going to sleep (15%).

Smaller proportions described notifications and messages (20%), procrastination (12%), negative emotions or stress (12%) as trigger, and habit or automaticity was even explicitly named a significant number of times (12%).
We first report three preregistered confirmatory hypotheses that concern between-groups comparisons of the detox and waitlist groups (RQ1-RQ3).
We then report the two remaining within-subject preregistered analyses, on the mechanisms underlying the detox effect (RQ4) and (self-reported) habitual slips during the detox (RQ5).
The detox significantly reduced social media use one week later (Figure 2a).

text.text: The detox was effective at reducing usage: participants in the detox group reduced their daily social media use by ~41 minutes (38.1%), from M = 107.2 minutes (SD = 61.0) at baseline to M = 66.4 minutes (SD = 58.0) one week post-detox (t(115) = 5.82, p < .001), whereas the waitlist group showed no meaningful change (M = 113.7, SD = 67.1 to M = 112.2 minutes, SD = 75.1; t(115) = 0.24, p = .81).

Our preregistered hypothesis (H3) was that craving would increase during the detox week.
Due to the unintentional omission of the BL1 craving survey in the waitlist group, the preregistered between-group test of during-detox change could not be conducted.

Notably, the within-subject test of H3 (Section 3.3.5), which is less severe than the preregistered between-group test, indicates that craving did not significantly increase during the detox, contrary to our prediction.
Here, we report on the between-group pre-post comparison.

text.text: As described in Section 2.4.1.2, we used the preregistered regression and an additional ANCOVA to test whether the reduction in SMU could be predicted by (i) change in automaticity, (ii) during-detox craving, and (iii) baseline motivation.

text.text: Within this model, automaticity change again predicted post-detox SMU (b = -8.47, SE = 4.10, p = .042), whereas during-detox craving (b = 7.95, SE = 5.81, p = .17), and baseline motivation (b = -11.98, SE = 7.91, p = .13) did not.
Overall, participants whose automaticity decreased more also reduced their social media use more, whereas during-detox craving and baseline motivation did not predict such a reduction.
This also answers our preregistered exploratory question on 'incubation' of craving: craving during the detox did not predict post-detox SMU.
In fact, craving did not increase during the detox (Section 3.3.5) and was reduced one week post-detox (Section 3.2.3).
In exploratory mediation analyses (Section 3.3.1), we therefore used post-detox craving (rather than during detox) and post-detox automaticity as mediators.
If social media use is habitual, removing the apps should provoke 'slips of action': cuetriggered actions that persist even when the goal (opening the app) is no longer reached.
To test this, we asked participants at the end of every day during the detox how often they reached for their phone to use social media, before realising the apps had been removed.
Nearly all participants (93.6%) reported at least one slip during the detox, with an average daily number of 2.30 slips (SD = 2.02) across the week.
As an exploratory first step, we examined how self-reported slips developed over the detox week (Figure 3b).

We additionally tested whether the effect of the detox on SMU was moderated by participants' baseline usage, automaticity, or craving.
We ran three separate regression models predicting post-detox SMU from group, a (mean-centered) baseline moderator, and their interaction.
Baseline SMU moderated the detox effect (Group × Moderator: b = 0.30, SE = 0.14, p = .034): the reduction in SMU was larger for participants with higher baseline use.

Finally, we examined whether the detox affected sleep, mental wellbeing and affective wellbeing (anxiety, depression, and stress).
All five measures showed a significant main effect of Time (all ps ≤ .041; Figure 5 and Supplementary Table S6), driven by two different patterns of results.

text.text: Mental wellbeing significantly improved during the detox week (d = 0.42), and sleep quality showed a small, non-significant improvement (d = 0.23, 95% CI [0.04, 0.42]; p = .057 after Bonferroni correction).
Both returned to baseline at one and three weeks post-detox.

In contrast, the DASS-21 symptoms showed more lasting reductions: anxiety, depression, and stress were all reduced during the detox (d = 0.49, 0.32, and 0.39) and remained significantly below baseline three weeks later (d = 0.25, 0.27, and 0.31).
Thus, the detox produced a temporary improvement in subjective sleep and wellbeing only during the detox, but a more lasting reduction in negative emotions.
Because these measures were only compared withinsubject, the changes cannot be attributed to the detox with certainty.

Moreover, the time course of mental wellbeing, anxiety and stress differed between groups (Group × Time, all ps ≤ .037; Supplementary Table S6): both groups improved during their detox, but only the immediatedetox group maintained these improvements afterwards, whereas the waitlist group returned to baseline.
