text.text: Can a brief social media detox provide a window of opportunity for breaking social media habits in individuals motivated to reduce their usage?

The present randomised controlled trial suggests the answer to this question is yes: a one-week detox significantly reduced subsequent social media use and subjective automaticity, and to a lesser extent craving, relative to a waitlist control group.
The reductions in use and automaticity persisted at three-week follow-up and remained evident at six months in a smaller subsample.
Importantly, as expected, participants whose automaticity decreased more also reduced their use more, consistent with the idea that the detox works (at least partly) by disrupting automaticity.
Several strands of evidence support the interpretation that the detox worked by disrupting habits.
First, the detox reduced not only social media use but also the automaticity of opening social media, and the size of this reduction predicted the reduction in use ( RQ4).
text.formatted: First, the detox reduced not only social media use but also the automaticity of opening social media, and the size of this reduction predicted the reduction in use ( <ref type="formula">RQ4</ref>).

text.text: An exploratory mediation analysis pointed in the same direction, although the indirect effect was not significant.

Second, although self-reported automaticity warrants some caution in interpretation (Hagger et al., 2015), our findings lend further credibility to the measure: baseline automaticity predicted self-reported slips of action during the detox week, mirroring experimental laboratory work (Watson et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Second, although self-reported automaticity warrants some caution in interpretation <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Hagger et al., 2015)</ref>, our findings lend further credibility to the measure: baseline automaticity predicted self-reported slips of action during the detox week, mirroring experimental laboratory work <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Watson et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Third, larger decreases in subjective automaticity were associated with larger increases in perceived control, consistent with automaticity and control representing opposing processes.
Finally, reductions in social media use were sustained at follow-up, in line with the detox successfully disrupting social media habits.

Together, these findings support the idea that -by removing behavioural accessibility -a social media detox can destabilise social media habits, creating an opportunity for lasting behaviour change in individuals motivated to change.

These findings add to existing evidence that the frequency of social media use is strongly associated with its automaticity (Anderson & Wood, 2025) and the self-reported habit strength of social media use is high (Sharpe et al., 2025).
text.formatted: These findings add to existing evidence that the frequency of social media use is strongly associated with its automaticity <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Anderson & Wood, 2025)</ref> and the self-reported habit strength of social media use is high <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Sharpe et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Contrary to our expectations, craving did not increase during or following the detox.
In hindsight, this is perhaps not surprising given our temporary, one-week abstinence period.
Incubation of craving effects have been primarily demonstrated in addiction contexts where abstinence is maintained over weeks to months (e.g. Parvaz et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Incubation of craving effects have been primarily demonstrated in addiction contexts where abstinence is maintained over weeks to months (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Parvaz et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Previous social media detox studies have reported mixed effects on craving, though most assessed it during or immediately after abstinence (Stieger & Lewetz, 2018; Wadsley & Ihssen, 2023; Wilcockson et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Previous social media detox studies have reported mixed effects on craving, though most assessed it during or immediately after abstinence <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Stieger & Lewetz, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Wadsley & Ihssen, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Wilcockson et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: We extend these findings by showing that craving remained reduced in the weeks following the detox, although this reduction was unrelated to changes in social media use.
Our findings contribute to the literature on what kind of interventions are likely to help, and for whom (Vanden Abeele et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Our findings contribute to the literature on what kind of interventions are likely to help, and for whom <ref type="bibr">(Vanden Abeele et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The detox was most effective for heavier users, although this partly reflects that they had more room to reduce.

The finding that a one-week detox produces lasting behavioural change, rather than merely suppressing use while access was restricted, is promising for detox interventions and addresses a gap in the literature, which is dominated by short-term or during-intervention outcomes.
Notably, our results speak to a broader question about how (digital) behaviour change interventions work.
Our detox can be contrasted with a recent intervention that disabled smartphone notifications for one week (Dekker et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Our detox can be contrasted with a recent intervention that disabled smartphone notifications for one week <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Dekker et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Unlike our detox, this did not reduce smartphone checking or screen time, nor improve perceived control, although it did reduce perceived checking-habit strength.

The authors offered two explanations: one week may be too brief to disrupt ingrained habits, or smartphone use is largely self-initiated rather than notification-driven, in line with naturalistic evidence (Heitmayer & Lahlou, 2021).
text.formatted: The authors offered two explanations: one week may be too brief to disrupt ingrained habits, or smartphone use is largely self-initiated rather than notification-driven, in line with naturalistic evidence <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Heitmayer & Lahlou, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Our findings argue against the first, as a one-week detox did produce lasting reductions, and are consistent with the second.

If the cues that drive social media use are largely internal, such as boredom, removing external cues such as notifications should have little effect, whereas removing access prevents the habitual response regardless of what triggers it.
Although this comparison is across studies, it suggests that removing access to the behaviour, rather than some of its cues, may be more effective in disrupting well-established social media habits.
Furthermore, the current detox -through temporary app removal -appears to be more effective than interventions that rely on planning (e.g. Brockmeier et al., 2025; Keller et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Furthermore, the current detox -through temporary app removal -appears to be more effective than interventions that rely on planning (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Brockmeier et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Keller et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: One explanation could be that such planning interventions mainly target self-regulatory processes, and that this does not work well for social media.

In contrast, approaches targeting automatic processes directly, such as adding friction through a brief pause before an app opens (Grüning et al., 2023), combining nudge-based interventions such as greyscale and disabling notifications (Olson et al., 2023), or personalised, automatic interventions specifically targeting habitual use (Roffarello & De Russis, 2021), seem to be more effective.
text.formatted: In contrast, approaches targeting automatic processes directly, such as adding friction through a brief pause before an app opens <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Grüning et al., 2023)</ref>, combining nudge-based interventions such as greyscale and disabling notifications <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Olson et al., 2023)</ref>, or personalised, automatic interventions specifically targeting habitual use <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Roffarello & De Russis, 2021)</ref>, seem to be more effective.

text.text: A detox fits into this second category, as it works on the automatic response (by removing behavioural access) rather than on the intention.

Our finding that reductions in social media use persisted for three weeks and (in a smaller subsample) up to six months, converges with Allcott et al. (2022), who found that a three-week financial incentive to reduce social media use produced reductions lasting six weeks after withdrawal.
text.formatted: Our finding that reductions in social media use persisted for three weeks and (in a smaller subsample) up to six months, converges with <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Allcott et al. (2022)</ref>, who found that a three-week financial incentive to reduce social media use produced reductions lasting six weeks after withdrawal.

text.text: While this is encouraging, in both cases usage did gradually drift back toward baseline, suggesting that a single disruption may not permanently reset a habit.
These findings suggest that periodically abstaining may be needed to maintain a desired level of use.
Another important consideration concerns the scope of the effects of the detox.
At all timepoints, total screen time decreased less than social media use, because it got replaced by other phone use -particularly during the detox.
This pattern is consistent with the broader media displacement literature (Vanden Abeele et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This pattern is consistent with the broader media displacement literature <ref type="bibr">(Vanden Abeele et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, phone pickups did not change at any point, which suggests that the internally triggered self-interruption that drives most smartphone interactions (Heitmayer & Lahlou, 2021) remained intact, with other applications displacing social media.
text.formatted: Moreover, phone pickups did not change at any point, which suggests that the internally triggered self-interruption that drives most smartphone interactions <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Heitmayer & Lahlou, 2021)</ref> remained intact, with other applications displacing social media.

text.text: Importantly however, despite the limited reduction in overall smartphone use, anxiety, stress, and (to a lesser extent) depressive symptoms did reduce up to three weeks after the detox, extending Calvert et al. (2025) who similarly found affective wellbeing improvements during a social media detox even as total screentime increased.
text.formatted: Importantly however, despite the limited reduction in overall smartphone use, anxiety, stress, and (to a lesser extent) depressive symptoms did reduce up to three weeks after the detox, extending <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Calvert et al. (2025)</ref> who similarly found affective wellbeing improvements during a social media detox even as total screentime increased.

text.text: These within-subject changes should be interpreted with caution, however, as only the immediatedetox group maintained them.
Mental wellbeing showed a subtle improvement during the detox, consistent with recent meta-analyses (Ansari et al., 2024; Lemahieu et al., 2025), but this effect was not sustained afterwards.
text.formatted: Mental wellbeing showed a subtle improvement during the detox, consistent with recent meta-analyses <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Ansari et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Lemahieu et al., 2025)</ref>, but this effect was not sustained afterwards.

text.text: This is consistent with evidence that mental health relates not to total smartphone use but to the automaticity and centrality of specific apps within users' smartphone routines (Turner, Gastelum, et al., 2026), which is precisely what our detox disrupted by specifically reducing social media.
text.formatted: This is consistent with evidence that mental health relates not to total smartphone use but to the automaticity and centrality of specific apps within users' smartphone routines <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Turner, Gastelum, et al., 2026)</ref>, which is precisely what our detox disrupted by specifically reducing social media.

text.text: The detox also improved participants' subjective relationship with social media, increasing perceived control and appropriateness of use, and reducing mindless use, without altering how much they liked the platforms.
We deliberately recruited participants highly motivated to reduce their usage.
This has several benefits: alongside practical advantages such as reduced dropout, it reflects the population most likely to seek out and benefit from such an intervention.

On the other hand, self-selection means our sample consists of precisely those most likely to adhere and to benefit, so our estimates likely represent an upper bound, rather than an average, on the effect in the general population (Vanden Abeele et al., 2025).
text.formatted: On the other hand, self-selection means our sample consists of precisely those most likely to adhere and to benefit, so our estimates likely represent an upper bound, rather than an average, on the effect in the general population <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Vanden Abeele et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, because automaticity and use were measured at the same timepoint, we cannot establish the direction of this effect.
Truly establishing a causal role of automaticity requires designs that manipulate it directly.
Furthermore, both automaticity and slips of action relied on self-report, and their association should be read with common-method variance in mind.
Future studies should assess the habit construct more directly, for example by measuring slips behaviourally rather than through selfreport.
Finally, the randomised comparison extended only to one week post-detox.
The effects at three weeks and six months rest on within-subject change, so we cannot rule out that part of the longer-term reduction reflects factors other than the detox.
Building on the present study, there are several promising directions for future research.
First, longer follow-up is needed to establish how durable these effects are.
Second, future work could examine the optimal form of a detox: how long, how often, and what to detox from (e.g. social media or smartphone use in general).
Full abstinence may not be necessary (Brailovskaia et al., 2023), and longer abstinence may not be better (Hall et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Full abstinence may not be necessary <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Brailovskaia et al., 2023)</ref>, and longer abstinence may not be better <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Hall et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Identifying the minimum effective dose is therefore an important next step, particularly given that spontaneously adopted disconnection strategies are not associated with reduced use (Dekker et al., 2026; Vanden Abeele & Nguyen, 2024).
text.formatted: Identifying the minimum effective dose is therefore an important next step, particularly given that spontaneously adopted disconnection strategies are not associated with reduced use <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Dekker et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Vanden Abeele & Nguyen, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Third, testing the detox in samples that vary in baseline motivation and habit strength would improve generalisability and help disentangle how much each factor contributes to lasting change.
Together, this could lead to concrete recommendations on how people can use a detox to change their social media habits.
Our findings also raise the question of which level of habit a detox actually targets.

Social media habits have been described as operating at multiple levels (Bayer et al., 2022), from broad contextual cues -which app or situation triggers use -to specific response tendencies, such as reacting to a notification versus scrolling a feed, to social media posting behaviour (Turner, Gunschera, et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Social media habits have been described as operating at multiple levels <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bayer et al., 2022)</ref>, from broad contextual cues -which app or situation triggers use -to specific response tendencies, such as reacting to a notification versus scrolling a feed, to social media posting behaviour <ref type="bibr">(Turner, Gunschera, et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The effect of a detox is blunt: completely removing apps disrupts the whole system at once, which precludes any claim about which specific component is responsible for the effects we observed.
A complementary route for future research would be to manipulate specific components of habitual use to identify the most effective levers for change.
In addition, we see value in developing more direct behavioural measures of habitual social media use.

Slips of action -mindless, habitual initiations of app use -are clinically relevant because these could help to reveal the distinct contribution of habitual processes to social media use, alongside motivational and goal-directed processes (e.g., seeking information or relief from boredom).

More broadly, social media and smartphone use offer a promising real-world model of high-frequency, low-effort habitual behaviour, in which behaviour can be directly measured in ecologically valid settings.
This could make a valuable contribution to the habit research field more generally, which currently lacks reliable models of habitual behaviour in naturalistic settings.

One concrete step in this direction is to measure automaticity of specific social media habits, rather than general opening automaticity, for example by identifying prominent personal triggers of social media use and assessing automaticity with respect to those specific triggers (e.g., "Going on Instagram when I'm feeling bored is something I do automatically").
Our findings point to several promising candidate triggers, including internal cues, most commonly boredom, and external cues, such as breaks, commuting, waking, going to sleep, or notifications.
Together, these findings offer support for the idea that social media use is highly habitual, and that a one-week detox was sufficient to destabilise it.
Critically, these effects were not confined to the detox period, but persisted for weeks and, in a subsample, were still evident six months later.
This suggests that the detox did not merely suppress behaviour temporarily but supported sustained behavior change through the disruption of social media habits.
In other words, it facilitated a recalibration in which usage becomes less automatic and mindless, more in line with users' intentions, and more within their control.
We hope the present work encourages further research into how digital disconnection can be optimised to support sustained digital wellbeing.

If participants indicated they made slips, we asked them to estimate the number of slips using four ordinal categories: 1-3, 4-6, 7-10, 10+.
To obtain a score that we could use for the analyses, each category was recoded to its midpoint (1-3 = 2; 4-6 = 5; 7-10 = 8.5).
Since the highest category (10+) has no upper bound, we (arbitrarily) recoded it to 12, which is likely a conservative estimate.
If participants indicated they did not experience making any slip, this was coded as 0.
The seven daily values were then averaged to get a weekly mean slips score.
For the negative binomial regression, we used the weekly total of the recoded daily values, with the number of completed daily reports as offset.

Four participants completed one of the weekly surveys twice.
In those cases, we first selected the more complete response, or, if both were complete, the first of the two responses.
Participants reported social media use, total screen time and number of pickups for each day of the preceding week from built-in tracking (Screen Time on iOS, Digital Wellbeing on Android).
Times were entered as "h:mm" and converted to minutes.
Although participants did not always fully adhere to the h:mm convention, we were able to convert most of the numbers.
Entries like "-", "X" or "nvt" were converted to "0".
Days without a value, or with a value that could not be converted, were treated as missing (~1% of entries).
If across all three usage types all fields of a week were 0 or "-", the week was treated as not reported.
In the total screen time field, some participants entered hours and minutes on some days, and one whole single number on others, making it unclear whether it reflected hours or minutes.
Numbers >16 were always considered to reflect minutes, but numbers between 1-16 were read as hours if that was closer 1.

text.text: The preregistered research question was whether automaticity, craving and motivation mediate the effect of the detox on SMU.
A preregistered exploratory question asked whether increased craving during the detox predicts post-detox use ('incubation' of craving).
The analysis plan, however, states the expected direction the wrong way around: "We expect smaller decreases in automaticity and bigger increases in craving to be predictive of detox success".

The analysis was run as preregistered (two-sided) and interpreted in the direction implied by the research question: bigger decreases in automaticity and smaller increases in craving predict larger reductions in use.
Because the test was two-sided, the mistake did not affect the test itself, only which direction of a significant effect counts as support.
That direction follows from the research question, which was fixed before data collection, so the correction added no flexibility.
We preregistered excluding participants who spent more than 20% of their baseline SMU during the detox, but did not define baseline.
The waitlist group had three baseline weeks.

We also preregistered sensitivity analyses "with and without participants who failed to be offline during the detox", without specifying whether this referred to the participants above the 20% criterion or to any use during the detox.
Baseline SMU was the mean of the two weeks before the detox for both groups, and this baseline was used in all analyses.

To obtain a more reliable baseline, the same was done for automaticity in the within-subject analyses; the between-group analyses used the single pre-detox week, and a two-week baseline gave the same result (Supplementary Section S3.5).

text.text: Because craving did not increase during the detox (Section 3.3.5) but did decrease following the detox (Section 3.2.3), we examined whether this post-detox reduction in craving mediated the effect on SMU, in a comparable manner as the automaticity analysis.

Group significantly predicted post-detox craving (a path: b = 0.43, SE = 0.15, 95% CI [0.13, 0.74]), but post-detox craving (corrected for baseline craving) did not predict post-detox SMU (b path: b = 8.49, SE = 5.35, 95% CI [-2.08, 18.90]).

The indirect effect of group on SMU via craving was therefore not significant (a × b: b = 3.66, SE = 2.68, 95% CI [-0.92, 9.52]), and the direct effect remained significant (c′ path: b = 37.14, SE = 8.97, 95%CI [19.66, 55.22]).

The total effect in this model (b = 40.79, SE = 8.60, 95% CI [23.80, 58.12]) differs slightly from that in the automaticity model because the baseline covariate differs (craving instead of automaticity).

Deviations from preregistration Deviations are classified following Lakens (2024). Deviation 1: Test of H3 (missing information)

We hypothesised that craving would increase during the detox (H3), but the analysis plan specified only a pre/post-detox mixed ANOVA, which tests change after the detox. No analysis was specified for change during the detox.

We tested H3 by comparing detox-craving with baseline-craving (i.e. within-subject), pooling both groups (Section 3.3.5). We had envisioned to also run a between-group version of this test, but this was not possible because the craving questionnaire was left out of the waitlist group's BL1 survey through an administrative error. Without a concurrent control group, the within-subject test cannot separate an effect of the detox from changes over time. The preregistered pre/post comparison (Section 3.2.3) and the analysis predicting change in SMU from craving during the detox (Section 3.2.4) were not affected. Deviation 2: 6-week follow-up (mistake in study execution)
We preregistered follow-ups at 6, 12 and 24 weeks. Due to an oversight, the 6-week follow-up was not sent.
Long-term effects are reported for 12 and 24 weeks. These analyses were secondary, so the confirmatory tests are unaffected. Deviation 3: Analysis model for RQ4 (mistake in the preregistration)
We preregistered a linear mixed model to predict pre-post change in SMU. Change scores yield one value per participant, so there is no nesting to model.

We used multiple regression, the single-level equivalent. This did not affect the severity of the test. As a non-preregistered check, we also report an ANCOVA predicting post- detox SMU from baseline SMU and the same predictors.
